scribe_response.text: Tell me about a teacher or a mentor who influenced you. The person who influenced me most, after my parents, was a chief engineer named Mister Duncan Hale. He was a Scotsman with white eyebrows and a voice like gravel in a bucket. I um met him in nineteen eighty-three, when I had been in Abu Dhabi for four years. He had worked on coastal plants in three continents, and he spoke of them as old friends. On my first day under him, he walked me around the plant without saying a word for an hour. At the, At the end he asked me what I had noticed, um and I gave a long technical answer. He um shook his head and said that I had looked at the machines but not at the men. I did not understand at first, and I felt a little stung. Later I saw what he meant, because the operators knew things that no drawing contained. One of them could tell by the pitch of a pump when a seal was about to fail. Mister Hale made me sit with those men for a week and simply listen. It was the best week of training I ever had. He taught me to keep a, a logbook with complete honesty, including uh my own mistakes. What happened next? He said that an engineer who hides an error is building a bridge with a missing bolt. I wrote my first mistake in the book soon after, a valve that I had left half open. He read the entry, gave me a nod, and never mentioned it again. In the evenings he would invite a few of us to his flat for tea and shortbread. He kept a shelf of old technical books, and he let us borrow them freely. He also played the bagpipes badly, which we all politely pretended to admire. He kept a small tin of peppermints on his desk and offered one to every visitor. He believed that every plant had a personality, and he named the pumps after Scottish rivers. Our largest pump was called the Spey, and it never failed him. The operators loved that habit, and soon um they were naming the valves too. I was amused to discover that he loved Carnatic music, which a colleague had played for him uh once. He asked me to bring him recordings, and uh I brought him a tape of a veena recital. On Fridays he lectured us for ten minutes on the history of water. Can you tell me more about that? He listened with his eyes closed and said that the music reminded him of well tuned machinery. I thought it was the nicest compliment a Scotsman could give. When a new contract required long nights, he worked right beside us, with his sleeves rolled up. He never raised his voice, and he never took credit for our ideas. When I was promoted to supervisor, he gave me a brass slide rule that had belonged to his own teacher. I still keep it in a drawer, wrapped in a soft cloth. He retired in nineteen ninety and went back to a small town near Aberdeen. We wrote to each other at Christmas for twenty years, and his letters were always short. The last one said only that the heather was in bloom and that he missed the heat. I felt a deep sadness when his daughter wrote to tell me that he had died. I try to treat my own juniors in the way that he treated me. I listen first, I give them real responsibility, and I let them make small mistakes. A good mentor is someone who makes you slightly better than you believed you could be. He did that for me, and I am grateful every time I, I open that drawer.
